metadata.title: Validating Radiology AI Model Performance on Photon-Counting CT Images Using Large Language Models for Ground Truth Extraction.
metadata.journal: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR

abstract:
OBJECTIVE
To evaluate the feasibility of using large language models (LLMs) to automate ground truth label extraction from radiology reports, enabling scalable assessment and monitoring of radiology artificial intelligence (AI) tools. The framework is tested by validating AI model performance on a newly installed photon-counting CT (PCCT) scanner.


METHODS
We retrospectively analyzed four FDA-cleared deep learning-based computer-aided detection and triage (CADt) tools targeting pulmonary embolism (PE), intracranial hemorrhage (ICH), cervical spine fractures (CSPFX), and vertebral compression fractures (COMPFX). Radiology reports from exams acquired on the new PCCT scanner and conventional scanners were processed using an LLM (Llama 3.3) to extract binary ground truth labels. AI outputs were compared to these labels to estimate performance metrics. Discrepant cases were adjudicated by three human annotators, with inter-rater reliability measured using Fleiss' Kappa test. Performance metrics were recalculated after partial human correction of LLM errors.


RESULTS
LLM-extracted labels enabled rapid performance assessment across all four diagnostic tasks. There were no statistically significant differences in performance between PCCT and non-PCCT cohorts. In discrepant cases, the agreement between LLM labels and final human annotations (κ = 0.731) was comparable to inter-reader agreement (κ = 0.720), supporting the reliability of LLM labeling.


CONCLUSION
LLMs can be used to automate ground truth label extraction from radiology reports, offering a scalable and efficient alternative to manual annotation. This method supports rapid local validation of AI tools, even in response to input drift from new imaging hardware.

In cases of disagreement, a fourth annotator (N.M.C.) adjudicated the final label to produce a combined human annotation. Agreement between the combined human annotations and the LLM-extracted labels yielded a Fleiss’s κ coefficient of 0.731, suggesting that LLM-derived labels were comparable in consistency with human consensus. Key Words Artificial intelligence  radiology  large language models  photon-counting CT  model validation  MLOps  ground truth extraction    Introduction As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into radiology workflows, a challenge has emerged: ensuring that these tools perform reliably and safely in clinical practice. Robust performance assessment, both before deployment and through ongoing monitoring, is essential to realizing the value of AI and maintaining clinician trust. As a result, performance assessment has become a cornerstone of machine learning operations (MLOps) in health care [1 ]. At our institution, we have deployed several deep learning–based computer-aided detection and triage (CADt) tools, conducted predeployment validation before their clinical use, and routinely performed performance monitoring to ensure continued reliability. AI performance is highly dependent on local factors such as disease prevalence, imaging protocols, scanner models, and patient demographics. Recognizing this, radiology organizations increasingly advocate for local validation using internal datasets, ideally with ground truth labels derived from expert radiologist review [2-4 ]. Although this manual process is considered the gold standard, it is also labor intensive and difficult to scale. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) offer a promising strategy to address this challenge. These models, which have demonstrated strong capabilities in understanding and generating complex medical language, are now being explored for a range of clinical tasks. In radiology, LLMs have been used to generate impressions, summarize findings, and structure free-text reports [5-9 ]. Although previous studies have applied natural language processing techniques to radiology reports for data curation [10 ,11 ], to our knowledge, no prior studies have described the use of LLMs to generate ground truth labels for AI performance evaluation. When a photon-counting CT (PCCT) scanner was installed at our institution as part of a clinical imaging upgrade, radiologists raised concerns regarding the compatibility of existing CADt tools. PCCT acquires images through mechanisms that differ substantially from those of conventional CT scanners [12 ], resulting in images that appear visibly distinct from those produced by conventional systems. Because the CADt tools were trained using data from conventional CT scanners, it was uncertain whether these tools can reliably generalize to the unique image characteristics of PCCT. In this study, we evaluated the feasibility of using LLMs to automate ground truth label extraction from radiology reports, using the validation of CADt tools on PCCT as a representative use case for scalable assessment and monitoring of radiology AI tools.  Methods Study Selection This retrospective study was conducted with approval from the institutional review board. Patients were identified using Epic’s SlicerDicer tool (Epic Systems Corporation, Verona, WI) within our electronic medical record system. To evaluate the generalizability of the clinical deep learning CADt tools implemented at our institution to a new PCCT scanner (NAEOTOM Alpha; Siemens), we extracted all examinations with AI results performed between the scanner’s installation and the beginning of the study period (April 28, 2025, to May 30, 2025). A control group was created by randomly sampling CT examinations from other scanners performed during the same time window. Some studies were excluded because of the absence of a valid radiology report. This occurred in cases such as procedural imaging not interpreted by a radiologist and external examinations archived without reinterpretation. The deep learning CADt models currently deployed analyze imaging studies immediately after acquisition and transmission to the PACS, with results integrated directly into the electronic health record, which also serves as our radiology information system. Examinations routed for AI CADt processing are initially filtered by modality and body part, while the vendor applies its own orchestration to determine whether an examination is appropriate for analysis. The models included in this study detect the presence or absence of the following findings on CT examinations: pulmonary embolism (PE), intracranial hemorrhage (ICH), cervical spinal fractures (CSPFX), and vertebral compression fractures (COMPFX).  Data Privacy and Deidentification Procedures After identifying the patient cohort for this study, all examination accession numbers and medical record numbers were replaced with a SHA-256 hashed version before any further processing or analysis. All dates were shifted.  Ground Truth Label Extraction With LLM The reports for each cohort were processed using an LLM (Llama 3.3; Meta Platforms), which was prompted to return a binary response indicating the presence or absence of the target pathology, formatted in JavaScript Object Notation. The methodology for prompting and processing using LangChain, Pydantic, and Ollama is described in prior work [13 ]. Revisions were then made to the prompt to ensure accurate extraction. The refinements generally included providing definitions of terminology, adding instructions for handling uncertainty and ambiguity, specifying how to address chronicity of findings, and clarifying how to differentiate between similar clinical scenarios or closely related terms. The complete compiled prompts used for each finding type are provided in Supplemental Material 1 . Cases were excluded if inference or parsing failed after two retries with error messages, for example, if the model output was not in a valid JavaScript Object Notation format. Inference times for each case were also recorded.  Evaluation of CADt Models By comparing CADt outputs against LLM-extracted labels, the performance of various AI models can be estimated with substantially less manual effort than traditional methods that rely on expert-curated annotations. In this study, four CADt models targeting distinct diagnostic tasks (PE, ICH, CSPFX, and COMPFX) were evaluated using this LLM-assisted approach. Given the number of reports being analyzed and the number of diagnostic tasks (4) it was impractical to manually review all reports by multiple annotators to fully evaluate the accuracy of LLM extraction. Thus, we had focused on manually adjudicating only studies in which the CADt outputs were discrepant to the LLM-extracted labels (ie, false-positive [FP] and false-negative [FN] groups in our initial analysis). Reports in these groups were manually adjudicated by three human annotators (M.M.K., W.E.K., Z.D.M.). The cases for which there was disagreement among the three annotators were adjudicated by a fourth independent annotator (N.M.C.). The performance of the CADt models was recalculated after correction of LLM extraction errors in the FP and FN classifications. This set of “corrected” performance metrics shows more of a best-case assessment of the CADt model, as there were presumably also LLM extraction errors that resulted in agreement with the CADt label (ie, true positives and true negatives) that were not evaluated by the manual annotation process.  Statistical Analyses Model performance metrics were calculated including sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value and F1 score. Ninety-five percent confidence intervals were estimated using bootstrapping. Because three independent human annotators reviewed the FP and FN (discrepant) subset of cases, Fleiss’s κ coefficient was used to analyze interreader reliability. Fleiss’s κ was also calculated to measure agreement between the adjudicated ground truth labels and the LLM-extracted labels. Analyses were performed primarily using the Python scripting language and the data science library scikit-learn. Graphs and figures were generated using the Python library seaborn.   Results Patient Selection During the study period (April 28, 2025, to May 30, 2025), a total of 1,341 radiologic examinations acquired on the PCCT scanner with AI results were identified. A small number of inappropriate examinations may still be analyzed by the AI. These include external examinations archived without reinterpretation and procedural imaging not interpreted by a radiologist. After applying exclusion criteria, the numbers of PCCT examinations included in the study were 601, 230, 207, and 761 for PE, ICH, CSPFX, and COMPFX detection, respectively. For the control cohort, 1,200 non-PCCT radiology examinations with AI results were randomly selected from the same time period (Fig. 1  ). Baseline characteristics of the radiology examinations included in this study are shown in Table 1  .   Evaluation of AI Models The evaluation results for the four AI CADt tools are summarized in Table 2  . The various performance metrics provide a comprehensive assessment of each model. The PE and ICH detection CADt demonstrated the highest performance in terms of the F1 score, a balanced metric that reflects both the positive predictive value and sensitivity. The F1 scores for PE and ICH detection CADt were 0.625 and 0.804, respectively, outperforming the CSPFX and COMPFX detection models, which had F1 scores of 0.300 and 0.573. These findings align with our clinical experience that the PE and ICH detection algorithms are the most clinically useful among the CADt tools currently implemented at our institution. Measurement of AI Performance on New Scanners Table 2  also summarizes the performance of the AI models on images acquired using the newly installed PCCT scanner at our facility compared with traditional non-PCCT scanners. The F1 scores for models applied to PCCT images were 0.765, 0.848, 0.432, and 0.450 for the PE, ICH, CSPFX, and COMPFX models, respectively. Notably, model performance was slightly higher, though not statistically significantly so, for three of the four AI models when evaluated on PCCT images compared with non-PCCT images. The Fisher exact test was used to compare each performance metric (sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value) between the PCCT and non-PCCT cohorts. None of these differences reached statistical significance. Confusion matrices for each model are shown in Figure 2  , with colors coded to scale. Side-by-side comparison of the confusion matrices provides a quick visual assessment, suggesting that CADt tools’ performance is generally similar on PCCT versus non-PCCT images.  Manual Adjudication of Discrepant Cases Fleiss’s κ among the three human annotators was 0.720, and the score between the final human annotation and the LLM-extracted labels was 0.731. This is illustrated in Figure 3  . Note that interreader agreement was not assessed between each individual human annotator and the final annotation, as the final annotation was derived on the basis of the initial human annotations. When pooling all cases from the FP and FN groups across the various CADt models, a total of 105 cases were reviewed by human annotators. Of these, 11 were determined to be truly discrepant, representing approximately 10% of the reviewed cases. With the labels in the FP and FN groups corrected through human adjudication, the performance metrics for each AI model were recalculated, as shown in Table 3  . There were no statistically significant differences between the metrics before and after partial human adjudication, as indicated by the overlapping confidence intervals. Visually, the confusion matrices before and after adjudication (Fig. 4  ) were similar. During the manual review of the reports and the LLM outputs, errors of LLM extraction often came from the LLM’s misinterpretation of nuanced clinical context. For instance, in the evaluation of spinal fractures, the LLM may incorrectly associate any pathologic description of a vertebral body, such as osteophytes or metastatic lesions, with an acute fracture in some cases. Similarly, procedural deferrals, such as the radiologist’s deferring to the dedicated spinal CT report for findings from a trauma pan scan, were misinterpreted as confirmation of a finding, even when the report explicitly stated that no fracture was identified. For ICH, the LLM failed to equate terms such as hypodense collection  with hemorrhage, while for PE, it struggled with temporality, misclassifying “resolved” or “previous” emboli as acute findings and failing to differentiate intravascular air from thrombus.   Discussion This study demonstrates the feasibility and utility of leveraging LLMs to support multiple facets of AI model evaluation and monitoring in radiology. Our results show that LLM-assisted evaluation can provide a reasonable approximation of model accuracy across a range of clinical tasks, including the detection of PE, ICH, CSPFX, and COMPFX. Importantly, we demonstrate that even with the small amount of error introduced by LLM-generated labels (comparable with human annotators), the performance metrics remain interpretable and clinically meaningful. The fact that several models, particularly the PE and ICH detection algorithms, continued to show strong performance under these conditions underscores the robustness of this approach. Our findings highlight the value of LLMs in ongoing model surveillance, an essential component of modern MLOps. In the case of the recently installed PCCT scanner, LLM-assisted evaluation enabled rapid confirmation that existing CADt models were performing similarly on this scanner’s data compared with existing conventional scanners, despite the CADt tools’ being trained on conventional data only. This allays radiologists’ concerns about CADt tools’ compatibility with PCCT scanners. The overall similarity in AI performance gave us confidence to approve the application of our existing algorithms to images acquired on the new scanner. These techniques can likely help organizations quantitate and navigate the growing concerns of AI bias and AI performance drift [14 ]. Our findings illustrate how LLMs can facilitate prompt, localized revalidation in response to system-level changes, thus, reducing reliance on manual workflows that may delay or prevent analysis. Despite these promising results, several limitations warrant discussion. First, the populations on the PCCT and the other scanners are inherently a little different. The PCCT is situated as one of the primary emergency department scanners for a large level 1 trauma center, and the other scanners handle a variety of case mixes from other emergency departments, inpatient settings, and outpatient settings. This may account for some of the differences seen in the data between these populations versus random sampling. Second, although LLMs reduce manual annotation, they are not infallible. Mislabeling by LLMs introduces uncertainty into performance estimates and may bias results. Although not all LLM-extracted labels were manually adjudicated, for cases in which the LLM-extracted labels were discrepant from the AI CADt tool outputs, we calculated interreader agreement between the LLM-extracted labels and the final human annotation (following a two-step human adjudication process) and found it to be comparable with the agreement among the initial human annotators. This suggests that LLM-extracted labels may be noninferior to manually curated labels, despite being dramatically less labor intensive to produce. Third, this study focused on a limited set of diagnostic tasks and scanner types; additional validation is required to assess whether these findings generalize to other imaging modalities, report styles, or institutions. Fourth, a more complex prompt was used to minimize error that was based on prior pilot work and requires some thought and initial testing with iteration (on an independent dataset) to debug. However, this usually identifies components of the labeling task that would need to be clarified for humans if the labeling were done manually. However, using those techniques allows the generation of a single prompt for a task that can be used longitudinally and spells out the assumptions and nuance of the annotation task. Finally, although our prompting strategies were iteratively optimized and demonstrated using a single model (Llama 3.3), systemic sources of error across all models stemmed from the LLM’s misinterpretation of nuanced clinical context, which highlight a common challenge: the model’s difficulty in parsing complex inferences, anatomic specificity, and the temporal evolution of disease. To address these systematic errors, future work will involve refining our prompting strategies and trying to generalize concepts that should be included in any prompt for radiology report extraction. In the future, expanding the explicit rules in the prompt should provide clearer guidance on handling deferred or historical findings as well as pathologic findings outside of the CADt’s scope. Providing more medical and radiology lexicon and jargon targeted to the task should also facilitate accuracy. Newer generations of models will likely better handle radiologist’s inferences and complex descriptions. In conclusion, this study demonstrates the feasibility of using LLMs to automate ground truth label extraction from radiology reports for the purpose of monitoring radiology AI tools. Using this framework, we validated the performance of four CADt models when applied to images acquired from the PCCT scanner, even though these models were originally trained on data from conventional CT scanners. This approach can be scalable to support other key aspects of MLOps. In a similar fashion, LLMs can assist in the initial validation of newly adopted AI tools by generating large, labeled datasets from retrospective reports. In addition, they can enable continuous postdeployment monitoring by tracking performance metrics over time. This monitoring framework supports early detection of issues related to data drift, imaging protocol changes, or system failures [10 ], allowing timely remediation before clinical consequences arise. LLMs offer a promising and pragmatic solution to one of the key bottlenecks in radiology AI deployment as well as a host of data extraction–driven research. As generative models continue to improve, their role in AI operations will likely expand, enabling more agile and data-driven governance of clinical AI systems.  Take-Home Points ▪ LLMs can automate ground truth label extraction from radiology reports, offering a scalable alternative to manual annotation and enabling efficient evaluation of radiology AI tools.  ▪ Manual review of discrepant cases confirms acceptable LLM error rates, and the conservative nature of the method ensures AI performance is likely to be underestimated rather than overestimated.  ▪ AI CADt tools generalizability across imaging hardware can be rapidly assessed, as demonstrated by successful validation of existing models on a new PCCT scanner without significant performance degradation. key_findings.claim: Four FDA-cleared CADt tools for PE, ICH, CSPFX, and COMPFX detection showed no statistically significant performance degradation when applied to photon-counting CT images versus conventional CT images

key_findings.claim: PE and ICH detection CADt tools substantially outperformed CSPFX and COMPFX detection tools across both scanner types

key_findings.context: Consistent with institutional clinical experience that PE and ICH CADt algorithms are most useful; three of four models showed slightly higher (non-significant) performance on PCCT vs non-PCCT

llm_extraction.methods_summary: Retrospective single-institution study (University of Washington, April 28–May 30, 2025). Four FDA-cleared deep learning CADt tools targeting PE, ICH, CSPFX, and COMPFX detection were evaluated. Radiology reports from 1,341 PCCT examinations (NAEOTOM Alpha; Siemens) and 1,200 randomly selected non-PCCT examinations were processed by Llama 3.3 (Meta) via LangChain/Pydantic/Ollama to extract binary pathology labels (present/absent) in JSON format. CADt outputs were compared against LLM-extracted labels to compute sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, and F1 score with 95% CIs via bootstrapping. Fisher exact test compared PCCT vs non-PCCT performance. Discrepant cases (FP+FN groups) were manually adjudicated by three independent annotators (Fleiss's κ for interrater reliability); disagreements resolved by a fourth annotator. Performance metrics were recalculated after correction of LLM errors in discrepant cases. Identifiers were SHA-256 hashed and dates shifted for deidentification.
llm_extraction.limitations: 1) Patient populations inherently differ between PCCT (primarily emergency/level-1 trauma) and non-PCCT cohorts (mixed emergency, inpatient, outpatient), introducing demographic and disease-mix confounding beyond scanner differences. 2) Only discrepant cases (FP+FN groups) underwent human adjudication; LLM errors producing incorrect true positives or true negatives were undetected, so corrected metrics represent partial rather than full correction. 3) Single institution with short study window (one month) limits generalizability to other sites, report styles, imaging modalities, or scanner models. 4) Only one LLM (Llama 3.3) evaluated; performance of other models not compared. 5) Prompt engineering required iterative optimization on a prior pilot dataset, representing upfront development effort. 6) Systematic LLM error categories identified qualitatively but not systematically quantified across all error types.

relationships.description: Extends prior BERT-based automated annotation of large radiology datasets by applying newer instruction-following LLMs specifically for AI model performance evaluation ground truth extraction
Extends feasibility work on privacy-preserving LLM (Vicuna) for radiology report labeling by demonstrating application in MLOps: ongoing AI CADt performance monitoring and hardware-change validation

Extends open-source LLM extraction from free-text radiology reports by operationalizing extraction as a scalable ground-truth pipeline for clinical AI validation rather than standalone information retrieval
Provides a concrete practical implementation of the medical MLOps framework for radiology AI, demonstrating scalable local validation as an alternative to manual annotation-dependent workflows
Demonstrates a practical tool for detecting and quantifying AI performance drift due to imaging hardware changes, directly addressing the data drift monitoring challenge identified by Sahiner et al.

methodology_details.approach: LLM-based automated binary ground truth label extraction from free-text radiology reports using Llama 3.3 via LangChain/Pydantic/Ollama. Iteratively optimized prompts return JSON-structured binary labels (pathology present/absent). CADt model performance estimated by comparing AI outputs to LLM labels; discrepant cases manually adjudicated by human annotators. Performance recalculated before and after partial human correction.
datasets: PCCT cohort: 1,341 radiology examinations from NAEOTOM Alpha (Siemens) PCCT scanner, University of Washington (April 28–May 30, 2025); after exclusions: 429 PE, 516 ICH, 548 CSPFX, 529 COMPFX
Non-PCCT cohort: 1,200 randomly sampled radiology examinations from conventional CT scanners, same time period; after exclusions: 601 PE, 230 ICH, 207 CSPFX, 761 COMPFX
Human adjudication subset: 105 discrepant cases (FP+FN) reviewed by 3 annotators + 1 adjudicator
metrics: Fisher exact test (PCCT vs non-PCCT comparison)
methodology_details.reproducibility_notes: Full prompts provided in Supplemental Material 1. Python pipeline using scikit-learn (metrics) and seaborn (figures). Deidentification via SHA-256 hashing of accession/MRN and date shifting. Two-retry policy for failed LLM inference or JSON parsing. LangChain/Pydantic/Ollama methodology described in prior work (Kanani et al., J Imaging Inform Med, in press). IRB approved.

domain_specific_fields.benchmark: Cross-scanner validation: 4 FDA-cleared CADt tools (PE, ICH, CSPFX, COMPFX) benchmarked on PCCT vs conventional CT using LLM-generated ground truth labels
domain_specific_fields.model_architecture: Llama 3.3 (Meta Platforms); local deployment via Ollama; LangChain for prompt orchestration; Pydantic for JSON output schema validation; binary classification (presence/absence) per pathology type
domain_specific_fields.dataset: Single-institution retrospective CT radiology reports (University of Washington), April–May 2025; 2,541 total examinations (1,341 PCCT + 1,200 non-PCCT); four diagnostic tasks evaluated
